title: From Business Culture to Great Depression: The Twenties
summary: The 1920s brought spectacular growth in autos, chemicals, radio, and household appliances, and American multinationals dominated world markets. Consumer culture—installment buying, movies, celebrity heroes like Lindbergh—redefined the good life, and the flapper symbolized a new personal freedom for women even as the Equal Rights Amendment split the feminist movement. But prosperity was uneven: farmers sank into depression, unions lost over 2 million members under the open-shop 'American Plan,' and some 40 percent of Americans remained poor. Government under Harding and Coolidge served business through tax cuts, high tariffs, and a conservative Supreme Court, while scandals like Teapot Dome exposed the era's corruption.

Cultural conflict defined the decade. The Sacco-Vanzetti case revealed deep nativist prejudice; the revived Ku Klux Klan claimed millions of members hostile to immigrants, Catholics, and Jews; and the Immigration Act of 1924 imposed national-origins quotas that slashed southern and eastern European immigration, barred Asians entirely, and invented the category of the 'illegal alien.' Prohibition and the Scopes evolution trial pitted Protestant fundamentalism against modern secular culture. In response, a modern civil-liberties movement was born: the ACLU formed in 1920, Holmes and Brandeis began defending free speech after Schenck, and Meyer v. Nebraska gave cultural pluralism constitutional footing. In Harlem, the Great Migration fed a cultural Renaissance whose writers proclaimed a defiant 'New Negro.'

Herbert Hoover's 1928 landslide over Al Smith, the first Catholic major-party nominee, seemed to ratify Republican prosperity. But in October 1929 the stock market crashed, exposing structural weaknesses—unequal incomes, farm distress, speculation, and a fragile international financial system. By 1932 output had fallen by a third and a quarter of workers were unemployed. Hoover's voluntarist 'associational action,' the Smoot-Hawley Tariff, and the belated Reconstruction Finance Corporation failed to stem the Great Depression, discrediting the business creed and preparing the way for a new liberalism.
big_ideas: The 1920s consumer economy—cars, credit, advertising, and mass entertainment—redefined freedom as private consumption while replacing thrift with installment buying.
Prosperity bypassed farmers, most industrial workers, and African Americans, and extreme concentration of wealth and banking left the economy fragile.
Harding and Coolidge aligned government firmly with business through tax cuts, high tariffs, anti-union policy, and conservative court rulings like Adkins v. Children's Hospital.
Nativism triumphed in the Sacco-Vanzetti case, the second Klan, and the 1924 national-origins quota law, which excluded Asians and created the 'illegal alien.'
Culture wars over Prohibition and evolution (the Scopes trial) pitted fundamentalist, rural Protestant America against a pluralist urban modernity.
A modern conception of civil liberties emerged in the 1920s through the ACLU, the Holmes-Brandeis free-speech dissents, and rulings like Meyer v. Nebraska that protected cultural pluralism.
The 1929 crash triggered the Great Depression, and Hoover's commitment to voluntarism and limited direct relief proved unequal to the catastrophe.

key_terms.def: Prosecution of two Italian immigrant anarchists convicted of a 1920 Massachusetts robbery-murder on thin evidence amid anti-radical hysteria; their 1927 executions symbolized nativist injustice.
Young urban women of the 1920s who flouted prewar conventions with bobbed hair, short skirts, smoking, drinking, and open sexuality, embodying a consumer-oriented personal freedom.
Constitutional amendment proposed by Alice Paul in 1923 to erase all legal distinctions based on sex; most women's organizations opposed it for threatening protective labor laws.
Harding-era scandal in which Interior Secretary Albert Fall took payoffs for leasing federal oil reserves to private companies, becoming the first cabinet officer convicted of a felony.
Employers' 1920s strategy pairing the union-free open shop with company-provided pensions and benefits, which helped shrink organized labor by over 2 million members.
Supreme Court decision striking down a women's minimum-wage law and retreating from Muller, reasoning that enfranchised women no longer needed special workplace protection.
Organization founded in 1920, growing out of wartime free-speech defense, that litigated landmark cases establishing legal protection for expression and dissent.
Ruling that upheld the Espionage Act using Holmes's 'clear and present danger' test; later Holmes-Brandeis dissents, beginning with Abrams, seeded stronger speech protection.
Protestant movement insisting on the literal truth of the Bible and battling religious modernism, Darwinism, and the era's loosened moral codes.
Tennessee prosecution of teacher John Scopes for teaching evolution; Clarence Darrow's grilling of William Jennings Bryan made it a national showdown between fundamentalism and modern secularism.

Reborn in 1915, a mass movement of perhaps 3 million native-born white Protestants—strong in the North and West—targeting immigrants, Catholics, Jews, and Blacks in the name of '100 percent Americanism.'

Law setting national-origins quotas that drastically cut southern and eastern European immigration, banned Asian immigration entirely, exempted the Western Hemisphere, and created the Border Patrol and the 'illegal alien.'
Flowering of Black literature, music, and art in 1920s New York—Hughes, McKay, Hurston, and others—that rejected racial stereotypes and expressed the protest spirit of the 'New Negro.'
Panic beginning on Black Tuesday, October 29, 1929, that wiped out over $10 billion in value, shattered confidence, and helped trigger the Great Depression.
Record-high tariff signed by Hoover that provoked foreign retaliation and shrank world trade, deepening the Depression.
Hoover's agency lending federal money to failing banks, railroads, and businesses—a major break with laissez-faire, though he still refused direct relief to the unemployed.

timeline.event: Prohibition takes effect; the ACLU is founded; Sacco and Vanzetti are arrested
Sacco-Vanzetti trial; emergency quota act temporarily restricts European immigration
Harding dies and Coolidge becomes president; Teapot Dome scandal unfolds; Adkins and Meyer v. Nebraska decided
Immigration Act imposes national-origins quotas and bars Asian immigration; Coolidge wins in a landslide over Davis and La Follette
Scopes trial in Dayton, Tennessee, dramatizes the fundamentalist-modernist conflict
Lindbergh flies solo across the Atlantic; Sacco and Vanzetti are executed
Hoover defeats Al Smith, the first Catholic major-party presidential nominee
Stock market crashes on Black Tuesday, opening the Great Depression
Smoot-Hawley Tariff raises duties to record levels and worsens the global slump
Reconstruction Finance Corporation created; Bonus marchers driven from Washington; unemployment reaches 25 percent

themes: Work, exchange, and technology: Mass production, consumer credit, and welfare capitalism built the boom, while unequal incomes and speculation set up the bust.
Politics and power: Pro-business Republican rule and a conservative judiciary rolled back Progressive regulation, and Hoover's voluntarism defined the limits of the pre–New Deal state.

American and national identity: Quota laws, the Klan, Prohibition, and Scopes fought over whether America would be a homogeneous Protestant nation or a pluralist one, while courts began protecting civil liberties.
Migration and settlement: The 1924 law closed the golden door to Europe and Asia even as Mexican migration grew and the continuing Great Migration made Harlem the capital of Black America.
Culture and society: The Harlem Renaissance, flappers, and the Lost Generation reshaped American cultural identity and its ideas of personal freedom.
